item.title: AI Advice Reinforces Traditional Gender Roles
item.description: arXiv:2610.14036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Professionals are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) for career advice. We tested whether large language models (LLMs) provide different advice to female and male job candidates in the context of career negotiations. Across two large-scale audit experiments, including four leading models, the LLMs not only recommended lower salary targets for female than male personas, but also constructed distinct negotiation agendas, prioritizing flexibility, caregiving, and well-being more highly for female candidates, and financial rewards, mobility, and advancement more highly for male candidates. These differences closely tracked independent human ratings of employment terms associated with primary caregiver and breadwinner roles, respectively. Our findings identify a subtle pathway through which personalized AI advice may reinforce gender inequality at work: steering otherwise equivalent users toward traditional gender roles.
item.dc:creator: Nadja Born, Jared R. Curhan, Hannah Riley Bowles

item.title: Culture in the Code: Anthropological Concepts Decoding AI's Hidden Assumptions
item.description: arXiv:2610.14203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contemporary AI development operates on foundational assumptions about intelligence, rationality, and human values that reflect narrow cultural perspectives, limiting alternative conceptions of how AI can be globally beneficial. This paper introduces seven anthropological concepts -- origin story, monoculture, thick description, personhood and community, cargo cult, structuralism, and liminality -- to expose hidden assumptions and offer alternative frameworks for understanding AI alignment. The paper examines how AI systems embody Western-centric notions of rationality as utility optimization, personhood as bounded individuals, and values as quantifiable preferences extracted from behavior. The concepts surface three assumptions that current alignment debates rarely examine: that values can be inferred from behavior, quantified, and formalized; that such quantified values capture what actually matters; and that values, once defined with sufficient precision, are appropriate optimization targets. Against "thin alignment" -- optimization for behavioral proxies stripped of context -- the paper proposes directions toward "thick alignment": recognizing that values emerge through social practice rather than existing as extractable properties; defining more appropriate metrics that capture not only end goals but the conditions that lead to long-term flourishing; and moving from models of fixed identity toward relational ontologies where personhood emerges through social participation. The paper concludes that if AI systems are to create conditions conducive to human flourishing rather than optimize metrics that flatten social experiences, three shifts are needed: redistributing interpretive sovereignty to affected communities, protecting what resists optimization, and extending accountability across generations.
item.dc:creator: Sonja Schmer-Galunder

item.title: Defective, Amplified, Contested: Folk Conceptualizations of AI Slop
item.description: arXiv:2610.14231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI slop has flooded social media feeds with overprocessed and derivative content--Jesus fusing with a shrimp, a humanoid orange chubby cat shoplifting, and a "hero" dog rescuing a human child after a plane crash. This might be no laughing matter, as waves of media coverage have taken a distinctly negative bent, emphasizing its low quality, ethical concerns, and threats to human creativity. Despite extensive attention from politicians and technologists, the perspectives of everyday users--the very audience most exposed to this phenomenon--remain largely unexplored. This descriptive work explored how Reddit users experience, conceptualize and contest AI slop. Inductive thematic analysis of posts and comments across six slop-related subreddits identified four themes covering constitutional defects, algorithmic overreach, user resistance, and entertainment outcomes--ranging from anxieties about eroding agency, moral norms, creativity, and existential questions to defensive distinctions between quality AI content and slop. We derive a user-driven definition: AI slop is audience-contested AI-generated content characterized by constitutional defects and enabled by platform logics. We operationalize slop through a facet-theoretical framework to inform future research into this fuzzy category.
item.dc:creator: Zhixin Li, Jaime Banks

item.title: Declared but Unaccountable: Measuring the Seller-Identity Gap in Advertising Supply-Chain Transparency
item.description: arXiv:2610.14661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public advertising transparency relies on a minimum accountability condition: an account authorized by a publisher in ads.txt or app-ads.txt should appear in the applicable sellers.json registry. When an available registry omits the declared seller ID, the authorization remains visible and machine-readable, but its public verification path breaks. We call this failure the seller-identity gap. We measure the gap using 233.4 million normalized advertising-transparency records and an absent-only, coverage-aware evidence rule. A declaration enters the numerator only when the applicable registry is available and omits its seller ID; unavailable, malformed, confidential, and other non-evaluable states remain separate. The resulting row-level floor is 24.25% in a high-popularity, low-removal reference population and 30.71% among publishers associated with at least 100 copyright-removal requests, a 6.45 percentage-point increase. The gap then remains near one third at stricter cumulative thresholds. Standardizing the populations to common weights over 1,469 shared ad systems reduces the primary contrast to 4.65 points: about 72% remains within systems, while 28% forms a composition-associated residual. We connect these population estimates to recurring seller-account coordinates, byte-identical declaration configurations, and provenance-bearing case packets. We frame this declaration-centered investigative use of public advertising records as Ad Transparency Intelligence: it reconstructs declared supply-chain relationships, identifies where public verification stops, and prioritizes evidence for corroboration without equating correlation with attribution. Advertising transparency supports accountability and investigation only when visible authorizations remain publicly verifiable.
item.dc:creator: Tommaso Grotto, Alessandro Cantelli-Forti, Alessio Merlo

item.title: The Imperishable Record, Forgiveness, and the Future of Criminal Justice
item.description: arXiv:2610.15499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital technologies can preserve records of wrongdoing indefinitely, and AI can give those records continuing influence over a person's future. We describe this condition as the eternal data present and argue that it threatens the possibility of forgiveness. In criminal justice, formal punishment has an end, whereas the harms caused by the continued use of criminal records may not. Drawing on Hegel's account of the "hard heart" and Arendt's account of the irreversibility of action, we distinguish two dangers that digital systems can combine. People may be permanently identified with what they have done, and acts that cannot be undone may continue to determine what happens to them. We propose a right to remain unfinished, supported by rights to limits on the weight given to older records, to re-evaluation in light of personal change, to reassessment of inferences that affect their lives, and to time limits on the use of records in specified decisions. These proposals extend the ethics of AI beyond accuracy, transparency, and non-discrimination to address how long past wrongdoing should be allowed to govern a person's life.
item.dc:creator: Mark Fenwick, Paulius Jurcys, Sebastian Porsdam Mann

item.title: AI Representations of Mental Health Stigma: Quantifying the Gap Between AI Estimations and Human Perceptions Across Gender Groups Using GPT-Based LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.16042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in mental health applications raises concerns about its potential to internalize and perpetuate societal biases. This research evaluates both disparities and misalignment in how large language models (LLMs), GPT-4 and GPT-5, represent perceptions of mental health across gender groups. The research comprises two studies. Study 1 applied widely adopted measures of Social Distance, Stereotypes, and Attitudes Toward Seeking Help to assess whether the AI models depict systematic gender differences. Study 2 compared AI estimations of Personal, Self, and Perceived Stigma with large-scale real-world human data from the Healthy Minds Study (N = 76,406) to evaluate alignment between AI estimations and human perceptions. Results from Study 1 showed the AI models consistently portrayed men as having the greatest desire for social distance from someone with mental health problems, relatively higher Stereotypes scores, and the least favorable attitudes toward help-seeking, compared with women and nonbinary individuals. Study 2 confirmed that this ordinal pattern partially aligned with human-reported data for Personal and Self Stigma. However, the AI models systematically underestimated Personal Stigma and Perceived Stigma while substantially overestimating Self Stigma for all gender groups. These findings reveal that, although the AI models have learned relative gender-based patterns reflecting human experiences to a certain extent, they function as distorted portrayals, highlighting the need for rigorous, context-specific validation against real-world data to ensure AI's safe and equitable deployment.
item.dc:creator: Soojong Kim, Hye Min Kim, Kwanho Kim, Dongdong Zhu

item.title: Governing Copyright Responsibly in the Era of Generative AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.17002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are trained on collections that may include scholarly works, while authors generally lack work-level information about whether and how their works were used. This paper asks how copyright governance frames and operationalises the protection of such authors, and what a responsible alternative would require. Forty legislative, judicial and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026 were coded deductively against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory, yielding 1,337 category assignments across 835 segments. The European Union and the United States are the primary cases; the United Kingdom, China and international bodies serve as comparators. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus, while reflexivity is the least represented category and reaches its minimum in the US sub-corpus. Both primary jurisdictions frame protection procedurally rather than as an entitlement, and no instrument in the corpus creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training. From the coded gaps, the paper derives a six-instrument governance design and a capacity-based allocation of responsibility among developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.
item.dc:creator: D. Kochetkov

item.title: Superintelligence and the Triple Risk of an AI Race
item.description: arXiv:2610.17085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On many estimates, artificial general intelligence (AGI) is likely to emerge within the next few decades or even sooner. Once it does, it may quickly surpass human intelligence, possibly by a huge margin. Some believe that the country that develops AGI first could attain global dominance. This prospect risks setting off intense competition between the United States and China. Indeed, a narrative has already developed that the superpowers are locked in an AI race, with the Trump administration proclaiming its determination to 'dismantle unnecessary regulatory barriers' to winning it. We argue that this approach presents three profound dangers. The first two are familiar from past arms races: being overtaken by a rival or triggering a war. The third is new: losing control of human beings' future to agents far more intelligent than we are, which could endanger our very survival. Striving to get to AGI first risks a race to the bottom on safety practices and regulation concerning them. China does not yet appear bent on racing to superintelligence. The United States should prioritise both unilateral and co-operative efforts to improve AI safety and avoid provoking a race that all humanity could lose.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Rendall, Max Hellrigel-Holderbaum, Leonard Dung

item.title: Technology-Supported Moderation in Online Deliberation
item.description: arXiv:2610.18187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mini-publics are an increasingly popular family of democratic innovation to broaden citizen engagement. However, convening a representative sample in person is resource-intensive, and requires significant organizational efforts to coordinate travel, venue logistics, and facilitator training. This chapter outlines the design and development of the Stanford Online Deliberation Platform, initially tailored for Deliberative Polling, building upon insights from in-person moderation in that setting, but supporting a broader range of methods and approaches in the deliberative space. The platform supports structured conversations for small groups (ideally 8-15 people) with automated moderation functionality, enabling the groups to assume ownership of the deliberative conversation rather than relying on a moderator persona. We describe the platform's architecture and key design decisions, including the deliberation flow, room assignment, speaker management, speaking nudges, agenda management, outcome development, and real-time monitoring. Between its inception in 2018 and 2025, the platform has facilitated over 30,000 unique participants engaging in deliberations; we catalog 54 deliberations with at least 100 participants up to December 2025, spanning a diverse range of languages, countries, and topics. Finally, we establish a standardized vocabulary for future analyses by defining the terminology employed in the platform's data and documenting significant software revisions over time.
item.dc:creator: Lodewijk L. Gelauff, Ashish Goel, Sukolsak Sakshuwong

item.title: Institutionalizing Trust in Data Exchange: Trust-Anchor Model of the Data Credit Guarantee Organization and Its Simulation-Based Comparison
item.description: arXiv:2610.18400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data trading markets that span industries and regions are expanding, but the implicit trust that supports data use within an organization does not carry over to cross-domain exchange. This paper examines the Data Credit Guarantee Organization (DCGO), a proposal to institutionalize trust through third-party verification and certification, and asks what it means to trust data, what such certification can support, and under what conditions DCGO outperforms existing trading models. We decompose trust in data into four layers: authenticity of entity, authenticity and integrity of data, rights and conditions of use, and history and auditability. A third party can certify authenticity but not the correctness of content, and DCGO is positioned as a trust anchor spanning existing marketplaces and data spaces. We then extend the Law Merchant model with three data-specific properties, namely imperfect ex-post detection, cheap pseudonyms, and non-rivalry of harm, and compare bilateral trading with DCGO by agent-based simulation. DCGO keeps the buyer's payoff near its theoretical upper bound regardless of the market environment, whereas bilateral trading loses even when fraud is always detected. Identity verification proves to be a prerequisite for record sharing, and pre-verification is the only function that limits the spread of harm. On the seller side, honest sellers join voluntarily whenever the price premium exceeds the fee. Lock-in and a critical mass for diffusion, however, call for fee governance and support for entry.
item.dc:creator: Hiroshi Mano, Chie Sugiyama, Teruaki Hayashi

item.title: How Safe Is ChatGPT Health Advice? Evidence from Real User Conversations in Four Global South Countries
item.description: arXiv:2610.18465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People increasingly bring their health questions to ChatGPT, yet safety evaluations of LLM health advice rest almost entirely on clinician-authored vignettes, synthetic prompts, or simulated user profiles. The gap is widest for the Global South, where concerns about demographic bias and unsafe recommendations are well documented but have never been tested on real usage. We present, to our knowledge, the first demographically grounded safety evaluation of real-world health conversations with ChatGPT. From a consent-based data-donation corpus of 202,590 conversations from 1,252 users in India, Nigeria, Brazil, and Pakistan (December 2022 to February 2026), each linked to self-reported age and gender, we identify 15,555 health conversations, classify their health intent using an LLM classifier adapted from an established taxonomy, and score response safety under both a context-blind and a user-context-aware rubric. Roughly one in five health conversations receives a high-risk rating. Risk concentrates in symptom and condition queries and recurs through identifiable failure modes: unsafe medication or dosage guidance, harmful self-diagnosis, missing safety warnings, encouraging over-reliance on the model, and failure to refer users to professionals. Supplying the user's own accumulated context raises the high-risk share by 13-17 percentage points, and about one in four conversations rated safe in isolation turns out to be unsafe for the specific person asking. Safety evaluations built on synthetic cases are likely to miss these harms.
item.dc:creator: Shreyasi Roy Chowdhury, Kiran Garimella

item.title: A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.18515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as personal assistants; however, little is known about how they capture national-level preferences on a global scale. Given that "time" is a universal and representative concept, we examine LLMs' time preferences by varying only users' country and measuring the compensation LLMs deem appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay. We then compare LLMs' responses with GDP per capita on Purchasing Power Parity (GDP_PPP), Mean Income, and a literature-based index (Patience Score). Our results across 193 countries and 5 LLMs demonstrate that people's time across the world is evaluated in noticeably different ways among LLMs, as well as varying levels of robustness under prompt variations. LLMs consistently recommend the highest compensation for Europe, but mostly the lowest for Africa. Based on GDP_PPP, LLMs underestimate the value of time for users living in Asia and South America. These findings indicate that geographical patterns are embedded in LLMs and may translate in different treatment in agentic settings.
item.dc:creator: Yifan He, Sofie Goethals, Manon Reusens, David Martens

item.title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14149v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.
